verdicts.trueWording: This information is entirely speculative (including the very claim
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via action=raw (HTTP 200, 220KB). Section 'Knowledge-cutoff disclaimers and speculation about gaps in sources' carries the sentence with 'speculative' wikilinked to WP:OR, so the rendered contiguous string matches the quote. The parenthetical continues with the claim that it is 'not documented', and the following sentence calls the low-profile variant speculative too. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Though the details of these resistance efforts aren't widely documented
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that 'Throwing Curves: Eva Zeisel' is a Wikipedia biography — the page names it only as the article the revision belongs to, and that article is about a 2002 documentary film, not a biography
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in the Examples box of the knowledge-cutoff section, attributed to 'this December 2024 revision' (Special:Diff/1261964722) to Throwing Curves: Eva Zeisel, with 'aren't widely documented' highlighted. December 2024 and the hedging function are supported. The 'biography' limb is not: the en.wikipedia extract for that title opens 'Throwing Curves : Eva Zeisel is a 2002 documentary film directed by Jyll Johnstone.'

verdicts.trueWording: citations are completely made up. The DOIs lead to different citations
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the commentary under the ChatGPT example in section 'DOIs that lead to unrelated articles'. The section's own opening sentence carries every limb of the claim in the guide's voice (non-existent scholarly articles, DOIs that appear valid but are assigned to unrelated articles).

verdicts.trueWording: LLMs often generate book citations that do not include page numbers
verdicts.note: Quote is the opening sentence of section 'Book citations without page numbers or URLs'. The 'cannot verify the prose' limb is supported by the commentary after the Ohm's-law example, which says that without the page number the citation is not useful for verifying the claims in the prose.

verdicts.trueWording: attribute opinions or claims to some vague authority
verdicts.note: Section heading is exactly 'Vague attributions and overgeneralization of opinions'. Quote verbatim in its first sentence (which names the practice weasel wording); the exaggeration limb is the immediately following sentence about exaggerating the quantity of sources those opinions are attributed to.

verdicts.trueWording: checked against original or reputable sources to ensure accuracy
verdicts.note: Live page fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200, 43KB) and stripped to text. Quote verbatim under heading 'Accuracy of Information' inside 'Concerns and Ethics with AI Genealogy'. Byline 'Abby Tanner' and date 'February 19, 2026' both present on the page, matching the source line.

verdicts.trueWording: transform dry details into a story or biographical format
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the 'Telling stories:' bullet under 'How Can AI Be Used for Genealogy?', framed as a benefit ('with AI, you can breathe life into the past'). The bullet itself says 'AI'; the 'generative AI' limb is supported earlier on the same page, whose Generative AI section states that when AI writes a short story it is using generative AI.

verdicts.trueWording: obituaries in which a person's family members get mixed up
verdicts.note: Live washingtonpost.com returned curl error 92 on HTTP/2 and stalled on HTTP/1.1, so route 2 was used: the Wayback raw capture web.archive.org/web/20250804135306id_/... (HTTP 200, 2.3MB) — the raw article page, not a summarizer. Quote verbatim in the sentence attributing it to the tools' tendency to hallucinate, inside the section headed 'Passed away peacefully'. Byline Drew Harwell; capture dated 2025-08-04 with 'Yesterday at 7:00 a.m. EDT', i.e. 3 Aug 2025.

verdicts.trueWording: not to use flowery language or make any assumptions about how
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Quote verbatim; the sentence continues 'a person died, such as that they "passed away peacefully" ... as the tool wrote during one of his early attempts.' The speaker is introduced two paragraphs earlier as James, a worker at a funeral home in Philadelphia who withheld his last name, and the sentence opens 'When he uses ChatGPT to make an obituary' — every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: We don't know that it was a peaceful death
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture, same paragraph as index 994. The direct quote continues 'though we'd like to imagine it was,' he said — which is precisely the imagined-rather-than-known limb.

verdicts.trueWording: despite being given none of that information
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. The preceding paragraph identifies the tool as 'The Tribute tool on a funeral home's website in Florida'; the next sentence says the AI tool, instructed to write a playful obituary for a spirited, funny and faith-filled fake person, said the man had been 'born on a chilly day' and died in a 'sunny embrace', then closes with the quoted clause. All limbs (funeral home's Tribute tool, fictional man, both fabrications, nothing supplied) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: it invented fake nicknames, preferences and life events
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Sentence opens 'In other prompts,' immediately after the Tribute-tool paragraph, so 'the same tool' and 'the fictional subject' hold; it goes on to say the tool declared the man had established a community theater and mentored a young comedian.

verdicts.trueWording: where the AI tool seemed to exaggerate or make things up
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Box headed 'What AI obituaries look like' states that the Post used the AI-writing tool CelebrateAlly to create four sample obituaries about a fictional man named Jimmy, with the prompts entered plus notes carrying the quoted clause. Count, fictionality, tool and annotation limbs all supported.

verdicts.trueWording: stilted messages that read as if they were ripped from LinkedIn
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Treadway said it — the LinkedIn simile is Harwell's paraphrase of Treadway's reaction, not words attributed to him; Treadway's own quoted line instead says the obits look like they were taken off a resume
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture; section heading 'Creative ideas for a graveside service' confirmed. Quote is verbatim, in the reporter's sentence 'But he's been saddened to see so many obits get replaced by ...'. Two limbs are softer than the claim: the attribution (paraphrase, not quotation) and the quantity ('so many obits', not 'the obituaries he now reads').

verdicts.trueWording: you can actually see the person through the writer's eyes
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. The quote is verbatim, prefaced 'In a traditional obituary,' and closed 'she said' — 'she' being Irina Raicu, introduced three paragraphs earlier as directing the internet ethics program at Santa Clara University. The passage sits above the '‘Passed away peacefully’' section break, matching the cited location.
